items.title: 6.9.2 n Harmonic Means between two Numbers

blocks.text: \(H_{1}, H_{2}, H_{3}, \dots, H_{n}\) are called \(n\) harmonic means (H.Ms.) between \(a\) and \(b\) if \(a, H_{1}, H_{2}, H_{3}, \dots, H_{n}, b\) are in H.P. If we want to insert \(n\) H.Ms. between \(a\) and \(b\), we first find \(n\) A.Ms. \(A_{1}, A_{2}, \dots, A_{n}\) between \(\frac{1}{a}\) and \(\frac{1}{b}\), then take their reciprocals to get \(n\) H.Ms. between \(a\) and \(b\), that is, \(\frac{1}{A_{1}}, \frac{1}{A_{2}}, \dots, \frac{1}{A_{n}}\) will be the required \(n\) H.Ms. between \(a\) and \(b\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
"Inserting" means filling the gap: after inserting \(n\) means, the list \(a, H_{1}, \dots, H_{n}, b\) has \(n + 2\) terms, with \(a\) the first term and \(b\) the \((n+2)^{\text{th}}\) term.
So the method in steps is:
1. Flip the ends: \(\frac{1}{a}\) and \(\frac{1}{b}\).
2. In the A.P. \(\frac{1}{a}, A_{1}, \dots, A_{n}, \frac{1}{b}\), use \(a_{n+2} = a_{1} + (n+1)d\) to find \(d\).
3. Write \(A_{1} = \frac{1}{a} + d\), \(A_{2} = \frac{1}{a} + 2d\), and so on.
4. Flip each \(A\) back: \(H_{1} = \frac{1}{A_{1}}\), \(H_{2} = \frac{1}{A_{2}}\), ...

blocks.text_alt: d equals (1 over b minus 1 over a) over (n plus 1)

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: The formula above (ours, from \(\frac{1}{b} = \frac{1}{a} + (n+1)d\)) gives the common difference of the A.P. of reciprocals at once. Notice the \(n + 1\): inserting \(n\) numbers creates \(n + 1\) equal gaps.

blocks.title: Example 25
blocks.problem: Find three harmonic means between \(\frac{1}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{17}\).
steps:
Given: the end numbers \(\frac{1}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{17}\); we must insert \(n = 3\) harmonic means.
To find: \(H_{1}, H_{2}, H_{3}\) so that \(\frac{1}{5}, H_{1}, H_{2}, H_{3}, \frac{1}{17}\) are in H.P.
Method: insert three A.Ms. between the reciprocals \(5\) and \(17\), then take reciprocals.

Step 1: Set up the A.P. of reciprocals
Let \(A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}\) be three A.Ms. between \(5\) and \(17\), that is,
\[5, A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}, 17 \text{ are in A.P.}\]
Why: the reciprocal of \(\frac{1}{5}\) is \(5\) and of \(\frac{1}{17}\) is \(17\); the H.Ms. are the reciprocals of these A.Ms.

Step 2: Use \(a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\) for the last term
\[17 = 5 + (5-1)d\]
\(\because a_{5} = 17\) and \(a_{1} = 5\).
Why: the A.P. has \(3 + 2 = 5\) terms, so \(17\) is its \(5^{\text{th}}\) term.

Step 3: Solve for \(d\)
\[4d = 12\]
\[d = 3\]
Why: subtract \(5\) from both sides (\(17 - 5 = 12\)) and divide by \(4\).

Step 4: The three A.Ms.
\[A_{1} = 5 + 3 = 8\]
\[A_{2} = 5 + 2(3) = 11\]
\[A_{3} = 5 + 3(3) = 14\]
Why: the A.Ms. are the \(2^{\text{nd}}\), \(3^{\text{rd}}\) and \(4^{\text{th}}\) terms of the A.P.

Step 5: Take reciprocals
\[H_{1} = \dfrac{1}{8},\ H_{2} = \dfrac{1}{11},\ H_{3} = \dfrac{1}{14}\]
Why: the H.Ms. are the reciprocals of the A.Ms.

Check:
\(\frac{1}{5}, \frac{1}{8}, \frac{1}{11}, \frac{1}{14}, \frac{1}{17}\) have reciprocals \(5, 8, 11, 14, 17\), which increase by \(3\) each time: an A.P. So the five numbers are in H.P.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(n\) H.Ms. between \(a\) and \(b\): \(a, H_{1}, \dots, H_{n}, b\) are in H.P.
2. Insert \(n\) A.Ms. between \(\frac{1}{a}\) and \(\frac{1}{b}\), then take reciprocals.
3. The A.P. has \(n + 2\) terms, so \(\frac{1}{b} = \frac{1}{a} + (n+1)d\).
4. Check: the reciprocals of the whole list must have a common difference.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Inserting A.Ms. between \(\frac{1}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{17}\) themselves: that gives arithmetic means, not harmonic means. Flip the ends first.
2. Counting terms wrongly: with \(3\) means the last term is the \(5^{\text{th}}\) term, so use \((5-1)d\), not \((3-1)d\).
3. Giving the A.Ms. \(8, 11, 14\) as the answer: the H.Ms. are their reciprocals.
